 1.1 What is an Operating System?

 An operating system (OS) is a program that acts as an intermediary between the user of a computer and the computer
 hardware. It manages the hardware resources, runs user programs and gives them a convenient, efficient and safe environment
 to execute in.


Objectives (goals) of an OS

 Objective Meaning

 Convenience Makes the computer easy to use – users work with files, windows and commands instead of raw hardware registers.

 Efficiency Uses CPU, memory and I/O devices in an efficient manner – no resource sits idle if a process can use it.

 Throughput Executes user programs and solves user problems; more jobs completed per unit time.

 Ability to Built so that new system functions can be developed, tested and introduced without interfering with existing service
 evolve (modular design).


Four components of a computer system

 Users (people, machines, other computers)


 Application programs (browser, compiler, word processor, games)


 OPERATING SYSTEM (controls & coordinates the hardware)


 Hardware (CPU, memory, I/O devices)


 Abstract view of the components of a computer system (ch01 / Unit 1 slides).

 OS as a resource allocator – manages all resources (CPU time, memory, files, I/O) and decides between conflicting requests for
 efficient and fair use.
 OS as a control program – controls execution of user programs to prevent errors and improper use of the computer.
 Kernel – “the one program running at all times on the computer”. Everything else is either a system program (ships with the OS)
 or an application program.
 Bootstrap program – loaded at power-up/reboot, stored in ROM/EPROM (firmware). It initialises the whole system, then loads
 the OS kernel and starts its execution.

 1.4 Computer-System Operation, Dual Mode and Protection
 Interrupt-driven: device controllers have a local buffer; the CPU moves data between main memory and the buffers; when a
 device finishes it raises an interrupt. A trap/exception is a software-generated interrupt (divide by zero, system call).
 Storage hierarchy: registers → cache → main memory → SSD/disk → tertiary (tape/optical). Going down: slower, cheaper, larger,
 non-volatile. Caching copies information from slower to faster storage; the cache is checked first (hit) and data is copied in on a
 miss.
 Multiprocessor systems (parallel / tightly-coupled): advantages are increased throughput, economy of scale and reliability
 (graceful degradation). Types: asymmetric (a master CPU assigns work) and symmetric (all CPUs peers).

 1.5 Basic Concepts: Processes, Files and System Calls

Process
A process is a program in execution – a passive program on disk becomes an active process when loaded into memory. It needs
resources (CPU time, memory, files, I/O devices). The OS creates/deletes processes, suspends/resumes them, and gives mechanisms
for synchronisation and communication. (Full treatment in Chapter 2.)

Files
A file is a named collection of related information on secondary storage with a contiguous logical address space. The OS maps files
to physical storage, organises them in directories and controls access. (Full treatment in Chapter 7.)

 1.6 Operating-System Structures
The structure of an OS is how its components are organised and inter-connected: simple, monolithic, layered, microkernel, virtual
machines, and today mostly hybrid.

Simple structure (MS-DOS)
Not well divided into modules; there is no user/kernel mode, so applications can bypass the OS and access hardware directly – one
faulty program can crash the whole system. Small, fast, single-user.

Monolithic structure
The entire OS runs as a single program in kernel mode: a collection of procedures linked into one big executable. Every procedure
can call any other, using direct function calls in one address space. Examples: early UNIX, Linux, BSD.

Layered structure
The OS is divided into layers; the bottom layer (0) is the hardware and the top layer (N) the user interface. Each layer uses only the
functions and services of lower layers and hides its data structures and operations from higher ones. First built this way: the THE
system.

Microkernel and hybrid systems
Microkernel (e.g. Mach, basis of macOS/Darwin): moves as much as possible from the kernel into user space; the kernel keeps only
minimal process, memory management and communication (message passing between client and servers). Easier to extend and
port, more secure/reliable (a failing server is not a kernel crash), but user-space communication overhead lowers performance.
Hybrid systems (Linux with loadable modules, Windows, macOS) combine approaches for performance, security and usability.

 and one address space lower layers

 Communication Direct function calls between any components A request must pass through every intermediate layer

 Performance Fast – no layer crossing, shared address space Slower – overhead of crossing layers; many layers
 degrade performance

 Modularity / Poor – tangled code, hard to add/remove features, High – change one layer without affecting others; easy

 Structure of an OS means how its components (scheduler, memory manager, file system, drivers, IPC) are organised and

How it is overcome

 Layered design – modules arranged in layers with clean interfaces, so each layer can be tested and changed separately.

 2.3 Process Operations, Context Switch and Process Types

Creation and termination
 Creation: a parent process creates children forming a tree identified by PIDs. In UNIX, fork() creates a child (a duplicate of the
 parent) and exec() replaces its memory with a new program; the parent may wait() for the child.

 Termination: a process executes its last statement and calls exit() ; status returns to the parent via wait() ; resources are
 de-allocated. A parent may abort a child (child exceeded resources, task no longer needed, parent exiting – cascading
 termination).
 Zombie process: terminated but its entry remains in the process table because the parent has not yet read its exit status.
 Orphan process: parent terminated first; it is adopted by init .

 CPU-bound process: spends most time on the CPU (running state); I/O-bound process: spends most time waiting for I/O (waiting
 state) with short CPU bursts.

Context switching

 A context switch is the saving of the context (state held in the PCB) of the running process and loading of the saved context of
 another process, so the CPU can switch from one process to another. Context-switch time is pure overhead – the system does no
 useful work while switching.

Goals: maximise CPU utilisation and throughput; minimise turnaround, waiting and response time; be fair. For non-pre-emptive and

 Method to solve any scheduling numerical:

 1. List processes with AT, BT (and priority).

 2. Advance a clock t. At every decision point write the set of arrived and unfinished processes.

 3. Apply the algorithm’s rule to pick one (ties: earlier arrival, then lower process number).

 4. Draw the Gantt chart; read CT from it (if CPU idle, jump to the next arrival and show an idle block).

 5. TAT = CT − AT; WT = TAT − BT; RT = first start − AT. Average each column.

 6. Check: ΣBT = busy time; for AT=0 ΣWT can be checked from the Gantt chart start times.

B. Shortest Job First (SJF) — non-pre-emptive

 SJF: from the processes that have already arrived, run the one with the smallest burst time, to completion. Gives the minimum
 average waiting time for a given set of jobs (optimal), is a greedy algorithm; ties are broken FCFS.


 Advantages: minimum AWT; good for batch jobs whose run times are known.
 Disadvantages: burst time cannot be known exactly in advance (it is predicted by exponential averaging of previous bursts);
 starvation of long jobs if short ones keep arriving (cured by aging).

D. Priority Scheduling (non-pre-emptive and pre-emptive)

 Priority scheduling: each process has a priority number (here smaller number = higher priority, as in the slides and papers); the
 CPU goes to the highest-priority ready process; ties are broken by FCFS. Non-pre-emptive: a new higher-priority arrival waits for
 the running process to finish. Pre-emptive: it takes the CPU at once. SJF is priority scheduling with priority = 1/burst.


 Advantage: important processes run first; pre-emptive priority suits real-time systems.
 Problem: starvation (indefinite blocking) of low-priority processes under a steady stream of high-priority ones. Solution: aging –
 gradually raise the priority of a process as it waits (e.g. +1 every 15 min).
 With equal arrival times, pre-emptive and non-pre-emptive priority behave identically.

E. Round Robin (RR) — pre-emptive, time-sliced

 Round Robin: FCFS with a time quantum q (10–100 ms typically). The ready queue is circular: each process runs for at most q; if
 unfinished it is pre-empted and goes to the back of the queue. Designed for time-sharing; no process waits more than (n−1)×q
 for its next turn; starvation-free.


 Small q: better response time but more context switches (overhead); large q: fewer switches, degenerates into FCFS; the usual
 rule: q should be large compared with context-switch time and about 80 % of CPU bursts should be shorter than q.
 Average turnaround is typically higher than SJF but response is better. Pure RR gives no priority.

F. Multilevel Queue (MLQ) and Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ)
MLQ: the ready queue is split into several queues by process type (e.g. system > interactive > batch); each queue has its own
algorithm (RR for foreground, FCFS for background) and a process is permanently assigned to one queue. Scheduling among queues:
fixed-priority pre-emptive (higher queue must be empty first – starvation possible) or time-slice (e.g. 80 % CPU to foreground RR,
20 % to background FCFS).

MLFQ: processes may move between queues according to behaviour: CPU-hungry processes are demoted to lower-priority queues,
I/O-bound and interactive processes stay high; long-waiting processes are promoted (aging). It is defined by: number of queues,
algorithm per queue, rule to upgrade, rule to demote, rule for the initial queue.

 2.8 Starvation and Aging

 Starvation (indefinite blocking): a ready process waits indefinitely because other, more favoured processes keep getting the
 CPU (priority scheduling, SJF/SRTF). Aging: gradually increase the priority of a process as its waiting time grows, so every
 process eventually becomes the highest-priority one.


Example of aging: if priorities range 127 (low) to 0 (high) and the OS lowers the number by 1 every 15 minutes of waiting, a priority-
127 process becomes priority 0 in about 32 hours – it cannot starve forever.

 Context switch is switching the CPU from one process to another. The state of the old process is saved in its PCB and the state

 Significance of the PCB in context switching

 1. An interrupt or system call occurs while P0 runs; the CPU enters kernel mode.

 2. The kernel saves the context of P0 – program counter, registers, stack pointer and state (Ready/Waiting) – into PCB0.

 3. The scheduler picks P1; the kernel reloads the saved context from PCB1 (registers, PC, memory map) and sets its state to
 Running.

 4. P1 resumes exactly where it stopped. The PCB is the only place the state is stored, so without it neither saving nor
 restoring is possible and multitasking could not work.

 Overhead: the system does no useful work during a switch, so its time depends on PCB size and hardware support (e.g.
 multiple register sets). The PCB also links the process into the ready and device queues.

 3.1 Principles of Concurrency
Central to modern OS design is managing multiple processes: multiprogramming (many processes on one CPU), multiprocessing
(many CPUs) and distributed processing. The big issue is concurrency – managing the interaction of all these processes. Concurrency
arises in multiple applications (time sharing), structured applications (a program as a set of concurrent processes) and in OS
structure (the OS itself is a set of processes/threads).

 Key term Meaning

 Atomic A function or action implemented as a sequence of instructions that appears indivisible – no other process can see an
 operation intermediate state; it either completes entirely or not at all.

 Critical section A section of code that accesses shared resources and must not be executed by more than one process at a time.

 Mutual Only one process may be in its critical section at a time.
 exclusion

 Race Several processes read/write shared data and the final result depends on the order in which their instructions
 condition interleave.

 Deadlock Two or more processes wait forever for an event that only another waiting process can cause.

 Livelock Processes keep changing state in response to each other but make no useful progress.

 Starvation A runnable process is overlooked indefinitely by the scheduler/synchroniser.



 3.2 Race Condition

 A race condition occurs when the outcome of an execution depends on the particular order in which the accesses to shared data
 take place. Example: processes P0 and P1 both call fork() ; the kernel variable next_available_pid is not protected, so
 the same PID could be given to two different processes.

 3.3 The Critical-Section Problem
Consider n processes P0…Pn−1, each with a critical-section segment that may change common variables, update a table or write a
file. Problem: design a protocol so that when one process is in its critical section no other is in its. Each process asks permission in an
entry section, runs the critical section, then an exit section, then the remainder section.

 do {
 /* entry section : request permission */
 critical section
 /* exit section : release permission */
 remainder section
 } while (true);


 Requirement Statement

 1. Mutual If Pi is executing in its critical section, no other process can be executing in its critical section.
 exclusion

 2. Progress If no process is in its critical section and some wish to enter, only processes not in their remainder sections take part
 in deciding who enters next, and this decision cannot be postponed indefinitely.

 3. Bounded There is a bound on the number of times other processes can enter their critical sections after a process has
 waiting requested entry and before that request is granted (no starvation).


Kernel code too has race conditions; kernels may be non-pre-emptive (no race on kernel data but poor response) or pre-emptive
(more responsive but must be designed carefully).

Interrupt-based solution (uniprocessor only)
Entry: disable interrupts; exit: enable interrupts. Problems: a critical section that runs for an hour blocks the whole system; processes
can starve; it does not work on multiprocessors (disabling interrupts on one CPU does not stop another CPU); gives user programs
power over the whole machine.


 3.4 Software Solutions for Two Processes
Assume load and store are atomic. Attempt 1 – strict alternation with one shared variable int turn :

while (true) {

 /* critical section */
 turn = j; /* give the turn to the other process */
 /* remainder section */
 }



 Correctness of strict alternation: Mutual exclusion is preserved (turn is 0 or 1, never both). Progress is violated: if P1 finishes
 and sets turn = 0 but P0 is in a long remainder section (or has terminated), P1 cannot re-enter even though the critical section
 is free – the processes are forced to alternate. Bounded waiting holds only while both keep alternating.


Peterson’s solution

 Peterson’s solution is a classic two-process software solution using two shared variables: int turn (whose turn to enter) and
 boolean flag[2] ( flag[i] = true means Pi is ready to enter). A process first announces interest, then politely gives the

 4.1 Principles of Deadlock

 A deadlock is a situation in which a set of blocked processes each holds a resource and waits to acquire a resource held by
 another process in the set; none can proceed because the event they wait for can be caused only by another waiting process.


System model: the system has resource types R1…Rm (CPU cycles, memory, files, I/O devices), each with Wi identical instances. A
process uses a resource in the order request → use → release. If the request cannot be granted immediately the process waits.

Four necessary conditions (Coffman conditions)
Deadlock can arise only if all four hold simultaneously:

 Condition Meaning Example

 1. Mutual Only one process at a time can use a (non-sharable) resource A printer or a mutex lock
 exclusion

 2. Hold and wait A process holding at least one resource is waiting to acquire additional P1 holds the scanner and asks for the
 resources held by others printer

 3. No pre- A resource can be released only voluntarily by the process holding it, after You cannot forcibly take a half-printed
 emption it has finished its task page back

 4. Circular wait There is a set {P0, P1,…, Pn} where P0 waits for a resource held by P1, P1 for P1 → R2 held by P2, P2 → R1 held by
 P2, …, Pn for P0 P1


How they lead collectively to deadlock: mutual exclusion and no pre-emption mean a held resource cannot be taken away; hold-
and-wait means processes keep what they have while asking for more; circular wait closes the chain so every process in it waits for
the next. Remove any one condition and deadlock is impossible. (Asked in 2024-25 Q7a and 2023-24 Q1c.)

 /* thread one */ /* thread two */
 pthread_mutex_lock(&first_mutex); pthread_mutex_lock(&second_mutex);
 pthread_mutex_lock(&second_mutex); pthread_mutex_lock(&first_mutex);
 /* work */ ... /* work */ ...


Deadlock occurs if thread one locks first_mutex and thread two locks second_mutex before either takes its second lock: each
now waits for the other (circular wait). Livelock is a variant in which processes keep changing state in response to each other
without making progress (two people stepping aside in a corridor), neither is blocked.

Banker’s algorithm (multiple instances)

 Banker’s algorithm: each process must a priori claim its maximum use; when it requests resources the system grants them only

 Data structure (n processes, m resource types) Meaning

 Available [m] Available[j] = k ⇒ k instances of Rj are free

 Allocation [n×m] Allocation[i][j] = k ⇒ Pi currently holds k instances of Rj

Safety algorithm

 1. Let Work and Finish be vectors of length m and n. Initialise Work = Available , Finish[i] = false for all i.

 2. Find an i such that Finish[i] == false and Needi ≤ Work . If none exists go to step 4.

 3. Work = Work + Allocationi ; Finish[i] = true ; go to step 2.

 4. If Finish[i] == true for all i the system is safe; otherwise unsafe.

Resource-request algorithm for Pi with request vector Requesti

 1. If Requesti ≤ Needi go to 2, else error (process exceeded its maximum claim).

 2. If Requesti ≤ Available go to 3, else Pi must wait (resources not available).

 3. Pretend to allocate: Available = Available − Requesti ; Allocationi = Allocationi + Requesti ; Needi =
 Needi − Requesti .

 4. Run the safety algorithm. If safe → grant (allocation is made final). If unsafe → Pi waits and the old state is restored.


 Complexity and drawbacks: Safety algorithm costs O(m×n2) operations. Drawbacks of avoidance: high overhead, requires
 maximum needs in advance, impractical for dynamic systems, low resource utilisation, limited scalability.

If neither prevention nor avoidance is used, the system must provide a detection algorithm and a recovery scheme. For single-

 1. Work = Available. For each i: if Allocationi ≠ 0 then Finish[i] = false, else Finish[i] = true.

 3. Work = Work + Allocationi; Finish[i] = true; go to 2.

 4. If Finish[i] == false for some i, the system is deadlocked and Pi is a deadlocked process. (Cost O(m×n2).)

 5.1 Background — Why Memory Management?
A program is permanently kept on the backing store (disk). To run it, it must be brought into main memory and placed inside a
process. The CPU can access directly only main memory and registers. The memory unit sees just a stream of addresses + read
requests or address + data + write requests. A register is accessed in one CPU clock (or less); main memory may take many cycles
and cause a stall; a cache sits between main memory and the CPU registers to hide this gap.

 Storage Speed Directly accessible by CPU?

 Registers one clock or less Yes

 Cache a few clocks Yes (hardware managed)

 Main memory (RAM) many cycles Yes – the only large store the CPU addresses directly

 Memory management is the OS function that keeps track of every memory location (free or allocated), decides which process
 gets memory, when and how much, and protects each process from the others. Main memory must hold both the OS and the
 user processes, so it is a limited resource that must be allocated efficiently. Goals: relocation, protection, sharing, logical
 organisation, physical organisation.


Protection with base and limit registers
Each process must be able to access only addresses inside its own address space. The simplest hardware support is a pair of
registers: the base register holds the smallest legal physical address and the limit register holds the size of the range. The CPU
checks every memory access generated in user mode: the address must satisfy base ≤ address < base + limit , otherwise
the hardware traps to the OS (addressing error). Loading the base and limit registers uses privileged instructions that only the OS
(kernel mode) may execute.

 5.3 Contiguous Memory Allocation
Main memory is usually divided into two partitions: the resident OS (normally in low memory together with the interrupt vector)
and the user processes (in high memory). Under contiguous allocation each process is contained in a single contiguous section of
memory. Relocation + limit registers protect user processes from each other and from changing OS code/data: the base (relocation)
register holds the smallest physical address, the limit register holds the range of logical addresses – each logical address must be
less than the limit; the MMU maps logical to physical dynamically. This also lets kernel code be transient and the kernel change size.

Fixed (static) partitioning
The number of (non-overlapping) partitions in RAM is fixed and made before execution (at system configuration); sizes may or may
not be equal. No spanning is allowed – a process must fit completely inside one partition. Each partition holds at most one process,
so the degree of multiprogramming = number of partitions.

 a whole partition

 Little OS overhead External fragmentation – free space scattered over partitions
 cannot be combined

 Process larger than the largest partition cannot run

 Limits the degree of multiprogramming

 Processes P1 = 1 MB, P2 = 7 MB, P3 = 7 MB, P4 = 14 MB occupy the four partitions. Internal fragmentation = (4−1) + (8−7) +

 free space is spread over four partitions (no spanning) → that 7 MB is lost to external fragmentation. A 32 MB process is invalid
 (bigger than the largest partition).



Variable (dynamic) partitioning
Partitions are not made in advance. RAM starts empty and a partition equal to the process size is created at run time, so no internal
fragmentation, no limit on process size (except total RAM) and no fixed limit on multiprogramming. Memory then contains holes –
blocks of available memory of various sizes scattered through memory. When a process arrives it is given memory from a hole large
enough; when it exits its partition is freed and adjacent free partitions are combined. The OS keeps a table of (a) allocated
partitions and (b) free partitions (holes).

 Advantages Disadvantages

 No internal fragmentation External fragmentation (holes appear as processes come and go)

 No restriction on degree of multiprogramming Harder to implement – allocation at run time

 No limit on process size Needs compaction or good placement algorithm

Segmentation is a memory-management scheme that supports the user’s view of memory: a program is a collection of segments. A

Segmentation architecture
 Logical address = a two-tuple <segment-number s, offset d> .

 Segment table – one entry per segment with base (starting physical address) and limit (length of the segment). It is itself stored

 STBR (segment-table base register) points to the segment table in memory; STLR (segment-table length register) gives the

 1. CPU generates <s, d>.

 4. Compare d with limit: if d ≥ limit → trap (addressing error); offsets lie in [0, limit−1].

5.5 Paging

 Paging is a non-contiguous, fixed-size partitioning scheme: the physical address space of a process can be non-contiguous; the
 process is allocated physical memory whenever it is available. Physical memory is divided into fixed-size blocks called frames
 (size is a power of 2, between 512 bytes and 16 MB); logical memory is divided into blocks of the same size called pages. The OS
 keeps track of all free frames. To run a program of N pages we need N free frames and load the program into them; a page
 table translates logical to physical addresses. Paging avoids external fragmentation and the problem of varying-sized memory
 chunks (but has internal fragmentation).


Address translation scheme
An address generated by the CPU is divided into page number p (index into the page table, which holds the base address (frame
number) of each page in physical memory) and page offset d (combined with the base address to give the physical address sent to
memory). For a logical address space of size 2m and a page size of 2n: the high-order m−n bits are the page number and the low-
order n bits are the offset.

 Page-table size number of entries (= number of pages) × entry size

Page table and its implementation
 The page table is a data structure mapping a page number to a frame number; each process has its own page table; number of
 entries = number of pages of the process. Each entry (PTE) also holds control bits: valid/invalid, protection (r/w/x), dirty,
 reference.
 It is kept in main memory. PTBR (page-table base register) points to it; PTLR (page-table length register) gives its size. The page-
 table address is PTBR + p×(entry size).
 Disadvantage: every data/instruction access needs two memory accesses – one for the page table and one for the
 data/instruction – and the page table can consume a lot of memory.
 Storing the table in registers is fast but registers are tiny (0.5k–1k entries), so the whole table lives in memory and a cache of
 recent entries – the TLB – removes the double access.

Translation look-aside buffer (TLB)
The TLB (also called associative memory) is a small, very fast hardware cache of page-table entries, typically 64 to 1,024 entries. It is
searched in parallel: given page number p, if p is in an associative register the frame number comes out immediately (TLB hit);
otherwise the frame number is read from the page table in memory (TLB miss) and the entry is loaded into the TLB for next time.
Replacement policy (LRU, FIFO, random…) is needed when the TLB is full; some entries can be wired down (permanent). Some TLBs

 5.6 Swapping
A process can be swapped temporarily out of memory to a backing store and brought back for continued execution. The total
physical memory space of all processes can then exceed real physical memory. The backing store is a fast disk large enough to hold
copies of all memory images of all users and must give direct access to them. Roll out, roll in is a swapping variant for priority-based
scheduling: a lower-priority process is swapped out so a higher-priority one can be loaded and executed.

 5.7 Virtual Memory
Background: code must be in memory to execute, but the entire program is rarely used (error-handling code, unusual routines, large
data structures) and not needed all at the same time. Executing a partially loaded program means: a program is no longer
constrained by physical memory; each program takes less memory while running so more programs run at once (higher CPU
utilisation and throughput, no increase in response/turnaround time); and less I/O is needed to load or swap programs.


 Virtual memory is the separation of user logical memory from physical memory. Only part of the program needs to be in
 memory for execution, so the logical address space can be much larger than the physical address space. It allows address spaces
 to be shared by several processes, more efficient process creation, more programs running concurrently and less I/O to load or
 swap. It is implemented by demand paging (or demand segmentation).


The virtual address space is the logical view of how a process is stored: it normally starts at address 0 and is contiguous. The stack
starts at the maximum logical address and grows down while the heap grows up; the unused space between them is a hole that
needs no physical memory until the heap/stack grows into a new page – this enables sparse address spaces, dynamically linked
libraries and shared memory (system libraries are shared by mapping them into the virtual address space; pages can be shared
during fork).

Demand paging
Instead of loading the whole process at load time, bring a page into memory only when it is needed (“lazy swapper” – never swaps
a page in unless it will be needed; the swapper that deals with pages is a pager). Benefits: less I/O, less memory, faster response,
more users. It is like a paging system with swapping. Reference to a page: invalid reference → abort; not in memory → bring it in.

Each page-table entry has a valid–invalid bit: v = legal and in memory; i = either not in the logical address space or legal but not
currently in memory. Initially the bit is i for all entries. If the MMU finds i during translation it raises a page fault (trap to OS).

 Steps in handling a page fault (Unit 5, slides 55–56)

 1. A reference to a page first traps to the OS (page fault) because its valid–invalid bit is i.

 2. The OS looks at another table (the PCB’s internal table) to decide: invalid reference → abort; just not in memory → continue.

 3. Find a free frame (from the free-frame list; if none, page replacement – see below).

 4. Schedule a disk operation to read the desired page into the new frame.

 5. When the read completes, modify the internal table and the page table – page now in memory, set validation bit = v.

 6. Restart the instruction that caused the page fault (the process continues as if the page had always been there).

 Pure demand paging – start a process with no pages in memory: the first instruction faults, and so does every other page on first
 access. A single instruction can touch several pages (fetch, decode, two operands, store result) → multiple faults. Programs show
 locality of reference, so the behaviour is acceptable.
 Hardware support: page table with valid/invalid bit; secondary memory (swap space); instruction restart – e.g. a block move
 whose source and destination overlap, or auto-increment/decrement addressing, needs special care (restart the whole
 operation / pre-touch pages / keep old values in registers).
 Free-frame list – pool of free frames for satisfying faults; frames are given using zero-fill-on-demand (contents zeroed before
 allocation). At start-up all available memory is on the free-frame list.

 Worst-case stages in demand paging (Unit 5, slides 60–61)

 1–4. Trap to OS; save user registers and process state; determine the interrupt was a page fault; check the reference was legal and find the
 page on disk

 5. Issue a read from disk to a free frame: wait in the device queue; wait for seek/latency; begin transfer

 6. While waiting, allocate the CPU to some other process

 7–9. Receive disk-completion interrupt; save the other process’ state; determine the interrupt was from the disk

 10–11. Correct page table and other tables to show the page is in memory; wait for the CPU to be allocated again

 12. Restore registers, process state and new page table, resume the interrupted instruction

Let p = page-fault rate (0 ≤ p ≤ 1). EAT = (1 − p) × memory access time + p × page-fault service time. The fault service time (disk read,
usually ~ 8 ms) is about 100,000 times a memory access, so even a tiny p hurts.

5.8 Page Replacement
When a page fault occurs and no frame is free (all frames are used by process pages and also needed by the kernel, I/O buffers etc.)
the OS must choose a victim page to evict. Page replacement prevents over-allocation of memory and completes the separation
between logical and physical memory: a large virtual memory can be provided on a smaller physical memory. Goal: the algorithm
with the lowest page-fault rate on first access and on re-access.

 1. Find the location of the desired page on disk.

 2. Find a free frame: if there is one, use it; otherwise use a page-replacement algorithm to select a victim frame; write the victim
 to disk if it is dirty and update the page and frame tables.

 3. Read the desired page into the (newly) freed frame; update the page and frame tables.

 4. Restart the instruction that caused the trap.

Note that there are potentially two page transfers per fault (write victim + read page), which increases the effective access time. The
modify (dirty) bit reduces this overhead: each page has a dirty bit set by hardware when the page is written; only modified pages
are written back, an unmodified victim is simply discarded.

reference string consists of page numbers only (not full addresses); repeated access to the same page immediately after it was

Ways the CPU talks to a device

Polling (programmed I/O)

For each byte of I/O the host runs a handshake with the controller using two bits: the controller’s busy bit (in the status register) and
the host’s command-ready bit (in the command register):

 1. Host reads the busy bit repeatedly until it is 0 – this is the busy-wait cycle.

 2. Host sets the write (or read) bit; for a write it copies the data into the data-out register.


Unit 6 — I/O & Disk Scheduling Made by Jay Naik Page 137 of 174

3. Host sets the command-ready bit.

 4. Controller notices command-ready, sets busy, reads the command and performs the transfer.

 5. When the transfer is done, the controller clears the busy bit, error bit and command-ready bit.

Step 1 is a busy-wait; it is reasonable if the device is fast, but inefficient if the device is slow – the CPU wastes cycles. If the CPU
switches to other tasks it may miss a cycle and the data are overwritten/lost. Polling itself can take as few as 3 instructions (read
status, logical AND to extract the status bit, branch if not zero).

Interrupts

Better when the device is ready only infrequently: the device raises a signal on the CPU’s interrupt-request line; the CPU checks the
line after executing every instruction; if an interrupt is signalled the CPU saves state and jumps to the interrupt handler, which
determines the cause, services the device and returns (the CPU restores state and resumes).

 Maskable interrupts can be ignored or delayed by the CPU (used for non-critical events); non-maskable interrupts signal
 unrecoverable events (e.g. memory error) and cannot be disabled.
 Interrupt vector – a table of handler addresses; the interrupt number is an index, so the CPU can dispatch to the correct handler
 without searching; interrupt chaining handles more devices than vector entries.
 Interrupts have priority levels, so a high-priority interrupt can pre-empt a low-priority handler; a context switch occurs at start
 and end of handling.
 The same mechanism is used for exceptions (divide by zero, protection error, hardware error), page faults (memory-access
 error) and system calls (a trap that makes the kernel execute the request).
 Multi-CPU systems can process interrupts concurrently if the OS is designed for it; interrupt handling is time-sensitive, frequent
 and must be fast.

 6.3 Kernel I/O Subsystem
 I/O scheduling – some I/O request ordering via a per-device queue; the OS tries for fairness (no application gets poor service)
 and some systems implement Quality of Service (e.g. IPQoS). The OS keeps a device-status table with an entry per device (type,
 address, state: idle/busy/not functioning) and a queue of waiting requests for each.
 Buffering – storing data in memory while it is transferred between devices or between a device and an application.
 Caching – a faster device (memory) holds a copy of data. Always just a copy; key to performance; sometimes combined with
 buffering.
 Spooling – holding output for a device that can serve only one request at a time (e.g. a printer) in a spool file on disk; jobs queue
 and are printed one after another so processes do not interleave their output.
 Device reservation – exclusive access to a device via allocate/de-allocate system calls – watch out for deadlock.
 Error handling and protection – OS handles transient failures (retry), reports errors; I/O instructions are privileged so that all I/O

Buffering in detail
Why buffer? (1) to cope with a speed mismatch between producer and consumer of a data stream (e.g. a modem/network much
slower than the disk: collect data in a buffer, write the whole buffer to disk in one operation); (2) to cope with devices that have
different data-transfer sizes (fragmentation and reassembly of network messages); (3) to maintain copy semantics – the data
written to disk are those at the time of the system call, even if the application changes its buffer afterwards (the kernel copies
application data into a kernel buffer first).

 Single and double buffering (Unit 6, slide 13)

Double buffering uses two buffers (kernel and user, or two kernel buffers): while one is being filled by the device, the other is being
emptied/processed, so producer and consumer overlap and the device is rarely idle. A buffer is either full / being processed or not
full / being used. Circular (ring) buffering generalises this to n buffers for bursty I/O. Buffers may vary in size.

Improving I/O performance (Unit 6, slides 17–18)
I/O is a major factor in system performance: it demands the CPU to run device-driver and kernel I/O code, causes context switches
due to interrupts, copies data and is especially stressful for network traffic. To improve: reduce the number of context switches;
reduce data copying; reduce interrupts by using large transfers, smart controllers and polling; use DMA; use smarter hardware
devices; balance CPU, memory, bus and I/O performance for highest throughput; move user-mode processes/daemons to kernel
threads.

Performance parameters
 Transfer rate – rate at which data flow between drive and computer (theoretical e.g. 6 Gb/s; effective, real, about 1 Gb/s).

Logical block addressing and non-volatile memory
Disk drives are addressed as a large one-dimensional array of logical blocks, the logical block being the smallest unit of transfer.
Low-level formatting creates the logical blocks on the physical media. The array is mapped onto the sectors sequentially: sector 0 is
the first sector of the first track on the outermost cylinder; the mapping proceeds in order through that track, then the rest of the
tracks in that cylinder, and then through the rest of the cylinders from outermost to innermost. Logical-to-physical translation is
difficult because of defective sectors (remapped to spares) and because the number of sectors per track is not constant (more on
outer tracks – constant linear velocity vs constant angular velocity).

Non-volatile memory (NVM) devices – if disk-like they are called solid-state disks (SSDs); other forms are USB/flash drives, DRAM-
disk replacements and storage built into phones. They can be more reliable than HDDs, are more expensive per MB, may have a
shorter life span, have less capacity, but are much faster; they have no moving parts, so no seek time or rotational latency; buses
can be too slow, so they connect directly to PCIe.

A disk can be divided into partitions (minidisks/slices); partitions can be RAID-protected; a partition can be used raw or formatted
with a file system (a volume, with its info kept in a device directory / volume table of contents).


 6.5 Disk Scheduling
The OS is responsible for using the hardware efficiently: for disk drives this means a fast access time and high disk bandwidth. Since
seek time ∝ seek distance, scheduling tries to minimise total head movement. Requests come from the OS, system processes and
user processes; each I/O request includes input/output mode, disk address, memory address and number of sectors. The OS keeps a
queue of requests per disk; an idle disk serves a request immediately, a busy disk makes requests queue, so optimisation algorithms
only make sense when a queue exists. Modern drive controllers do much of this themselves (LBA, built-in queues of varying depth),
but the algorithms below are the foundation.

 (1) DMA – Direct Memory Access. For large transfers, programmed I/O (the CPU watching status bits and feeding the device

 DMA transfer.

 1. The device driver is told to transfer disk data to buffer address X, count C.

 2. The driver tells the disk controller to transfer C bytes from disk to the buffer at X; the DMA controller registers (address,
 count, control) are set.

 3. The disk controller starts the transfer and sends each byte to the DMA controller.

 4. The DMA controller writes the bytes to the buffer, incrementing the address and decrementing C until C = 0 (cycle stealing:
 it borrows memory cycles from the CPU).

 5. When C = 0 the DMA controller interrupts the CPU.

 Advantage: one interrupt per block instead of one per byte, so the CPU is free for other work.

Choosing an algorithm; Linux deadline scheduler
 SSTF is common and has a natural appeal (but may starve requests).
 SCAN and C-SCAN perform better for systems with a heavy load on the disk; less starvation, though still possible. Performance
 depends on the number and types of requests and on the file-allocation method (contiguous files cause little head movement,
 indexed/linked files cause more).
 Linux deadline scheduler avoids starvation: it keeps separate read and write queues and gives read priority (processes are more
 likely to block on reads than writes). It maintains four queues: two read and two write – one read and one write queue sorted in
 LBA order (essentially C-SCAN), and one read and one write queue in FCFS order. All I/O requests are sent in batches sorted in
 one queue’s order; after each batch it checks whether any request in the FCFS queues is older than a configured age and, if so,
 the next batch is taken from that queue.
 On SSDs there is no seek, so FCFS-like (e.g. NOOP) scheduling is used, merging adjacent requests.

 A file is a named collection of related information recorded on secondary storage – to the user the smallest allotment of logical

 executable file.

Information about all files is kept in the directory structure, which is maintained on the disk; both the directory structure and the
files reside on disk. A directory entry consists of the file’s name and its unique identifier, which locates the other attributes (on disk

 Sequential and direct access (Unit 7, slides 11–13)

Sequential access (the simplest, most common – editors, compilers): information is processed in order, one record after another.
Operations: read next (read the record at cp and advance cp), write next (append at the end and advance), reset (to the
beginning); some systems can skip forward/back n records; no read after the last write (rewrite). Based on a tape model but works
on disks as well.

Direct (relative) access: the file is a numbered sequence of fixed-length logical records, so a program can read/write any record in
any order. Operations: read n , write n , position to n followed by read next / write next , rewrite n , where n =
relative block number (relative to the beginning of the file; the first block is 0). Relative block numbers let the OS decide where the
file is placed and prevent the user from touching other files. Ideal for databases and large tables where immediate access to large
amounts of information is needed.

 sequential access implementation for direct access

 reset cp = 0;

 read next read cp; cp = cp + 1;

 write next write cp; cp = cp + 1;


Sequential access can thus be simulated on a direct-access file (table above, slide 14) but not efficiently the other way round. Index
and relative files (slide 15): other methods are built on top of direct access. An index (like the index of a book) contains pointers to
the blocks; to find a record, search the index first (binary search if sorted) and then use the pointer to access the file directly. If the
file is huge, the index itself is too big for memory → create an index for the index file (a primary index points to blocks of the
secondary index – e.g. IBM ISAM). Example: a file of 120,000 records of 64 bytes (7.68 MB); with 1,024-byte blocks there are 16
records/block → 7,500 blocks; an index with one 4-byte key-pointer pair per block fits in 30 KB – it stays in memory and a lookup
needs 1 disk read.

A disk can be subdivided into partitions (minidisks, slices); disks or partitions can be RAID protected against failure; a disk or

7.5 File Sharing and Protection
Sharing of files on multi-user systems is desirable and may be done through a protection scheme; on distributed systems files may
be shared across a network (e.g. NFS). A multi-user system needs user IDs to identify users (permissions and protection are per-
user) and group IDs that allow users to be in groups, permitting group access rights. Every file/directory has an owner and a group.

Remote file systems
 Use networking to allow file-system access between systems: manually via programs like FTP; automatically and seamlessly
 using distributed file systems; semi-automatically via the World Wide Web.
 Client–server model: clients mount remote file systems from servers; a server can serve multiple clients; client and user-on-
 client identification is insecure or complicated.
 NFS is the standard UNIX client–server file-sharing protocol; CIFS is the standard Windows protocol; standard OS file calls are
 translated into remote calls.
 Failure modes: remote file systems add failure modes (network partition, server crash) → protocols (stateless NFS) allow
 recovery; consistency semantics specify when modifications by one user become visible to others (UNIX semantics: immediately;
 session semantics (AFS): on close; immutable shared files).

Protection — access control
The file owner/creator should control what can be done (read, write, execute, append, delete, list) and by whom. Approaches:
access-control list (ACL) – for each file/directory a list of users and the access allowed (flexible; but variable-length lists and long);
access modes with three classes (UNIX): owner, group, public/others × r, w, x = 9 bits. Windows uses ACLs managed through a
graphical interface (Windows 7 ACL management, slide 28: add users/groups and tick Allow/Deny for each permission).

The file system must allocate the disk blocks of a file so that disk space is used effectively and the file can be accessed quickly. The
disk is a sequence of fixed-size blocks; a file occupies a set of blocks. Three major methods exist: contiguous, linked and indexed.

Each file occupies a set of contiguous blocks on the disk. The directory entry stores just the start block and the length (number of
blocks). A file of n blocks starting at b occupies b, b+1, …, b+n−1; logical block i is at physical block b + i.

 Describe any two file allocation methods in detail, along with diagrams and examples. [10 marks]
 The file system must allocate the disk blocks of a file so that space is used effectively and the file is accessed quickly. Two
 methods are described in detail (the third, indexed allocation, is compared at the end).

 1. Contiguous allocation. Each file occupies a set of contiguous blocks; the directory entry stores the start block and the
 length. Logical block i is at physical block start + i.

 Contiguous allocation on a 32-block disk
 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
 count count f f
 8 9 10 11 12 13 14 15
 tr tr
 16 17 18 19 20 21 22 23
 tr mail mail mail mail mail
 24 25 26 27 28 29 30 31
 mail list list list list


 Contiguous allocation: count (0, 2), f (6, 2), tr (14, 3), mail (19, 6), list (28, 4).

 Example: file mail starts at 19 with length 6: logical block 3 → physical 19 + 3 = 22; logical block 6 is outside the length → error.
 A new file of 8 blocks cannot be placed although 15 blocks are free (holes of 4, 6, 2, 3): external fragmentation, cured by
 compaction.

 Advantages Disadvantages

 Simple; fast direct and sequential access (one seek) External fragmentation

 Minimal head movement File size must be known; growth is difficult


 2. Linked allocation. A file is a linked list of disk blocks that may be scattered anywhere; every block holds a pointer to the next
 block; the directory stores the first (and last) block.

 Linked allocation: file jeep: 9 → 16 → 1 → 10 → 25
 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
 jeep
 8 9 10 11 12 13 14 15
 jeep jeep
 16 17 18 19 20 21 22 23
 jeep
 24 25 26 27 28 29 30 31
 jeep


 Linked allocation: file jeep = 9 → 16 → 1 → 10 → 25.

 Example: block size 512 B, pointer 4 B → 508 data bytes per block. Logical byte 1000: block index 1000 div 508 = 1, offset 492
 → second block of the chain = block 16; reaching it needs 2 disk reads (blocks 9 and 16).

 Advantages Disadvantages

 No external fragmentation; file can grow freely Only sequential access (i reads to reach block i)

 Size need not be known in advance Pointer space and a lost pointer loses the rest of the file


 Comparison with indexed allocation (all pointers of a file collected in one index block, e.g. index block 19 = [9, 16, 1, 10, 25]):
 direct access with one extra read and no external fragmentation, but an index block is needed for every file.

 7.7 Free-Space Management and File-System Implementation
The OS keeps a free-space list of all disk blocks not allocated to any file or directory. Creating a file searches the list and removes the
blocks from it; deleting a file adds its blocks back.

 Method How it works Pros / cons

 Bit vector One bit per block: 1 = free, 0 = allocated (or reverse) Simple; easy to find contiguous free blocks; bitmap
 (bitmap) must be kept in memory for speed – large for big disks

 Linked list Free blocks are linked; a head pointer to the first free block; No waste of space; but traversing the list is slow (one
 each free block holds the pointer to the next read per block)

 Grouping The first free block stores addresses of n free blocks; the first Many free blocks found quickly
 n−1 are free, the last holds the address of another such block

 Counting Store the address of the first free block and the count of Short list when free space comes in runs
 following contiguous free blocks (entries kept in a B-tree)

 Space maps Per-region log of allocate/free operations in a counting format, Scales to huge file systems
 (ZFS) replayed into an in-memory structure



 Bit-vector example
 Disk of 32 blocks; free blocks are 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 17, 18, 25, 26, 27. Bit vector (block 0 on the left, 1 = free):

 00111100 11111100 01100000 01110000


 Finding the first free block: scan words for the first non-zero word; block number = (bits per word) × (number of 0-valued
 words) + (offset of first 1 bit). Here with 8-bit words the first word is non-zero and its first 1 bit is at offset 2 ⇒ block 2. If the
 first two 8-bit words were 00000000 00000000 and the third 00100000, the first free block would be 8 × 2 + 2 = 18.

 Bitmap size: 1 TB disk with 4 KB blocks → 240/212 = 228 blocks = 228 bits = 225 bytes = 32 MB of bitmap.



File-system structure and implementation
The file system is built in layers: application programs → logical file system (manages metadata: directory structure, file control
blocks, protection) → file-organization module (knows files, logical and physical blocks; allocation; free-space manager) → basic file
system (issues generic commands to the device driver, e.g. “read drive 1, cylinder 73, track 2, sector 10”; buffers/caches) → I/O
control (device drivers and interrupt handlers) → devices.

 Directory structure per file system Per-process open-file table – pointer into the system-wide
 Per-file File Control Block (FCB / inode) – permissions, dates, owner, size, table, with file position and access mode
 pointers to data blocks Buffers holding file-system blocks


Opening a file: search the directory (cache first) → copy the FCB into the system-wide open-file table (count = 1, or count + 1 if
already open) → create an entry in the per-process table (file position, access mode) → return an index (file descriptor / handle) to
the process. Closing: remove the per-process entry; decrement the system-wide count; at 0 write the FCB back to disk if changed
and drop the entry.

 Summarize the main file attributes managed by a file system and explain the common operations that can
 be performed on a file. [5 marks]

 Attribute Meaning

 Name Only human-readable information

 Identifier Unique number identifying the file in the file system

 Type Kind of file (text, executable, …)

 Location Pointer to the file’s blocks on the device

 Size Current (and maximum) size

 Protection Who may read, write, execute

 Time, date, user ID Creation, last modification, last use – for security and usage monitoring


 These attributes are kept in the directory entry. Operations:

 Operation What happens

 Create Find space, add a directory entry

 Write Write at the write pointer, update pointer

 Read Read at the read pointer, update pointer

 Reposition (seek) Move the current-file-position pointer; no I/O

 Delete Release file space and erase the directory entry

 Truncate Erase contents, keep attributes

 Open / Close Load the directory entry into the open-file table / write it back

 A. Formulas and rules

 Topic Formula / rule

 CPU scheduling TAT = CT − AT; WT = TAT − BT; RT = first run − AT; CPU utilisation = busy time / total time; throughput = processes / time

 Scheduler choice FCFS (non-pre-emptive, convoy) • SJF (min AWT, non-pre-emptive) • SRTF (pre-emptive SJF) • Priority (aging cures starvation)
 • RR (q, no starvation; large q = FCFS)

 Critical section Mutual exclusion + Progress + Bounded waiting; semaphore wait(S): S--, block if < 0; signal(S): S++, wake one

 Producer– full = 0, empty = N, mutex = 1; producer: wait(empty), wait(mutex), insert, signal(mutex), signal(full)
 consumer

 Deadlock Mutual exclusion, hold & wait, no pre-emption, circular wait (all four together)
 conditions

 Banker’s Need = Max − Allocation; Total = Σ Allocation + Available; Work = Available; pick i with Needi ≤ Work; Work += Allocationi;
 request: Request ≤ Need and ≤ Available, then pretend-grant and test safety

 Address Physical = relocation + logical (check logical < limit); paging: p = addr div page size, d = addr mod page size, PA = frame × page
 translation size + d; segmentation: PA = base + d if d < limit

 Paging sizes Pages = process size / page size; address bits = log2(size); page-table size = entries × entry size; internal fragmentation
 (average) = ½ page

 TLB EMAT = h(c + m) + (1 − h)(c + 2m); with c = 0: h·m + (1 − h)·2m

 Demand paging EAT = (1 − p)·m + p·(page-fault service time); hit ratio = hits/refs; miss ratio = faults/refs

 Page FIFO = oldest; LRU = least recently used (look back); OPT = used farthest in future (look ahead); Belady’s anomaly only in FIFO-
 replacement type algorithms

 Swapping Swap time = process size / transfer rate (+ latency); context switch with swap = swap out + swap in

 Disk access Seek + rotational latency (½ × 60/RPM) + transfer (size / rate); disk capacity = surfaces × tracks × sectors × sector size

 Disk scheduling Head movement = Σ |ci − ci−1|; SCAN to disk end; LOOK to last request; C-SCAN/C-LOOK add the return jump

 File allocation Contiguous: block i = start + i; linked: data per block = block − pointer; indexed: max size = (block/pointer)²-levels × block;
 bitmap size = blocks / 8 bytes
